speaker: Tri Dao
title: Tri Dao: The End of Nvidia's Dominance, Why Inference Costs Fell & The Next 10X in Speed
question: In LLM serving, what technical breakthroughs drove the dramatic drop in inference costs over recent years?
guest: The other side is inference optimization, and we've been seeing an explosion of techniques there. In the early days, as a whole, we didn't understand what the bottlenecks of inference were. After a while, people realized it's a lot about data movement—moving the weights in and out of memory, and moving the KV cache, which is the part of the attention operation where you store the entire history to make the next prediction. So a lot of optimizations are around how to reduce data movement. For example, you can quantize the model. Two or three years ago, it was typical to use 16 bits per parameter, but now 8 bits is pretty common and some new models are using 4 bits, with research even exploring 1 or 2 bits. You see this really compelling trade-off: as you quantize the model, a lot of times you pretty much don't lose any quality. That requires fairly sophisticated techniques, but it has worked amazingly well.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The drop came from compounding gains across the stack rather than one breakthrough; by one widely cited estimate (a16z's "LLMflation"), the price of a fixed capability level has fallen roughly 10x per year.

On the model side, distillation and better training produced small models that match older large ones, so GPT-4-class quality now runs on a fraction of the parameters. Quantization (16-bit down to 8- or 4-bit weights) cut memory and compute with little quality loss, and mixture-of-experts architectures activate only part of the network per token.

On the serving side, continuous batching (popularized by vLLM and TGI) keeps GPUs saturated, while KV caching, PagedAttention memory management, and prompt caching eliminate redundant computation. FlashAttention and optimized kernels sped up attention itself, and speculative decoding uses a small draft model to accelerate a large one.

On the hardware side, each GPU generation (A100 to H100 to Blackwell) improved throughput per dollar, joined by custom accelerators from Google, Groq, and Cerebras.

Finally, open-weight models and provider competition compressed margins, so these efficiency gains passed through to prices.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
The dramatic drop in LLM inference costs stems from breakthroughs across memory management, kernel design, quantization, scheduling, and model-system co-design. Early serving engines wasted GPU capacity through static batching and contiguous key-value (KV) cache allocation. Continuous batching and PagedAttention eliminated memory fragmentation via virtual-memory paging, while prefix caching reused KV states across shared prompts to multiply concurrency. Meanwhile, FlashAttention cut high-bandwidth memory traffic through SRAM tiling, and Grouped-Query and Multi-head Latent Attention compressed KV caches directly.

Simultaneously, weight and KV quantization—progressing from INT8/INT4 schemes like AWQ to hardware-native FP8 and FP4—eased the memory-bandwidth bottleneck of autoregressive decoding. Modern serving clusters also use prefill-decode disaggregation and chunked prefill to separate compute-heavy prompt processing from memory-bound token generation, alongside speculative decoding to verify multiple drafted tokens in one forward pass. Paired with sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing, distillation into smaller models, and higher-bandwidth accelerators, these innovations increased serving throughput per dollar by orders of magnitude.

noweb.answer: The dramatic drop in LLM inference costs stems from co-designed breakthroughs across model architecture, serving systems, quantization, and hardware. Architecturally, sparse Mixture-of-Experts models decoupled total parameter capacity from per-token compute, while Grouped-Query Attention and Multi-Head Latent Attention drastically shrank the memory-bound key-value cache. At the systems layer, FlashAttention reduced memory traffic via IO-aware kernel fusion, and PagedAttention eliminated key-value cache fragmentation to unlock much larger batch sizes. Paired with continuous batching and disaggregated prefill-decode scheduling, modern engines keep accelerators saturated across concurrent requests without sacrificing latency. Serving-time optimizations such as prefix caching, which reuses attention states across shared prompt prefixes, and speculative decoding further eliminated redundant compute and relieved memory-bandwidth bottlenecks during token generation. Simultaneously, advances in quantization enabled near-lossless inference at FP8 and 4-bit precision, slashing memory footprints so large models fit on far fewer chips. Finally, distillation compressed frontier-level reasoning into smaller models, while new generations of AI accelerators delivered steep gains in high-bandwidth memory, native low-precision tensor throughput, and high-speed chip-to-chip interconnects.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Several software and hardware advances drove the drop together. The first group targeted memory. PagedAttention (vLLM) cut KV-cache fragmentation, and FlashAttention made attention aware of memory input/output (IO). Grouped-query and multi-query attention, and later DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention, shrank the KV cache so far more requests fit on one GPU. Continuous (in-flight) batching kept GPUs busy instead of waiting for whole batches to finish. Quantization to INT8, FP8 and now FP4 (via GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant, plus native FP8/FP4 on Hopper and Blackwell) cut memory and bandwidth needs, which matters because decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. Speculative decoding (draft models, Medusa, EAGLE) produced several tokens per expensive forward pass. Prefix caching, splitting prefill from decode, and better parallelism raised utilization further.

The second group was the models themselves. Mixture-of-experts designs like Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 activate only a small share of their parameters per token. Distillation and longer training let much smaller models match older frontier quality. Faster hardware and price competition among providers did the rest, which is why the price for a fixed level of capability has fallen roughly tenfold or more each year.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: The dramatic drop in LLM inference costs came from compounding breakthroughs across model architecture, numerical precision, serving systems, and hardware. At the model level, sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures decouple total capacity from per-token compute, while Grouped-Query Attention and Multi-head Latent Attention shrink the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive quantization—moving from FP16 to FP8, INT4, and FP4—slashed memory bandwidth and compute requirements with minimal quality loss. On the systems side, FlashAttention reduced slow high-bandwidth memory reads, PagedAttention eliminated KV-cache fragmentation to unlock far larger batch sizes, and continuous batching kept GPUs saturated across variable-length requests. Modern serving stacks further cut costs through prefix caching to reuse shared KV states, prefill-decode disaggregation to match compute-bound and memory-bound phases to optimal hardware, and speculative decoding to verify multiple tokens per forward pass. Combined with faster accelerators featuring higher memory bandwidth and native low-precision tensor cores, these innovations reduced per-token serving costs by orders of magnitude.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The biggest gains came from doing less work per token and getting more tokens out of each accelerator. Quantization moved model weights, activations, and sometimes the attention cache to lower precision, cutting memory traffic and letting more requests fit on a chip. Newer GPUs and custom accelerators made those low-precision operations faster and supplied more memory bandwidth.

Serving software raised utilization. Continuous batching lets new requests join as others finish, while PagedAttention allocates the key-value cache in blocks so more requests can run concurrently. FlashAttention reduces memory transfers during attention, prefix caching skips recomputation for shared prompt text, and speculative decoding lets a large model verify several tokens proposed by a cheaper model in one pass.

Models also got cheaper to run at a given quality level. Better training and distillation made smaller models practical for more tasks, and mixture-of-experts models activate only a fraction of their parameters for each token. Together, these advances reduced the accelerator time needed per token.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Inference got cheaper because each accelerator could serve more tokens per second, and smaller models could deliver quality that once required larger ones.

Continuous batching lets new requests join as others finish, keeping accelerators busy even when responses vary in length. PagedAttention reduces wasted memory in the key-value cache, which stores information from earlier tokens, so more requests can share one accelerator. FlashAttention cuts data transfers between accelerator memory and the compute cores. Lower-precision formats and quantization shrink model weights, reducing the memory traffic needed to generate each token.

Newer accelerators added memory bandwidth and faster low-precision arithmetic. Model design helped too. Distillation improved the quality of smaller models, while mixture-of-experts architectures let large models use only a fraction of their parameters for each token. The gains compound, though their relative importance depends on the model, request lengths, and traffic volume.
